summary: This Project presents a functional, two-state hydraulic model demonstrating the cardiovascular fluid shifts that occur during spaceflight and their physiological consequences. The model physically simulates the transition between Earth's gravity (1G) and the microgravity environment (0G simulation) of spaceflight. The project addresses a fundamental challenge in human spaceflight: understanding and visualizing how the absence of gravity redistributes bodily fluids, leading to the well-documented "puffy face, bird legs" phenomenon, cardiac muscle atrophy, and orthostatic intolerance upon return to Earth. By creating a closed-loop hydraulic system that can be oriented vertically (simulating Earth) or horizontally (simulating space), students can directly observe and measure these physiological changes in real-time. When astronauts enter microgravity, the normal gravitational gradient that pulls blood toward the lower extremities disappears. Baroreceptor activation: Pressure sensors in the neck and chest detect increased blood volume and signal the kidneys to excrete excess fluid. Reduced blood volume: Total circulating volume decreases by 10-15% within the first few days of spaceflight. Orthostatic intolerance: Upon return to Earth, astronauts frequently experience dizziness and fainting because their reduced blood volume and deconditioned cardiovascular system cannot maintain adequate cerebral perfusion.
details:
Model Design and Operation

The hydraulic model consists of a closed-loop fluid system mounted on a hinged board that can transition between vertical (Earth mode) and horizontal (spaceflight simulation) orientations. The system replicates the major components of the human circulatory system:

Components:

  • Central Pump ("Heart"): A squeeze bulb representing the left ventricle, requiring manual compression to circulate fluid
  • Vascular Network: Clear vinyl tubing representing blood vessels, with Y-connectors splitting flow to upper and lower body regions
  • Head Reservoir: A clear balloon or pouch that visibly expands with fluid accumulation
  • Leg Reservoirs: Two elongated balloons or tubes that demonstrate fluid pooling under gravity
  • One-Way Valves: Aquarium check valves simulating heart valves and preventing backflow
  • Working Fluid: Red-dyed water representing blood

Two-State Operation:

Earth Mode (Vertical Orientation): Gravity pulls fluid downward into the leg reservoirs. The student must squeeze the heart bulb forcefully and frequently to push fluid upward against gravity into the head chamber, demonstrating the normal cardiac workload required to maintain cerebral perfusion.

Spaceflight Mode (Horizontal Orientation): When the board is laid flat, the vertical gravitational gradient is eliminated. Fluid immediately redistributes from the legs into the central chest and head chambers. The head reservoir visibly expands above the Earth baseline mark, physically demonstrating the cephalad fluid shift experienced by astronauts.

Investigation Protocol

The project includes a three-part demonstration protocol that systematically explores cardiovascular physiology across gravitational states:

Test A — Earth Physiology (Vertical): Establishes baseline fluid distribution and demonstrates the cardiac effort required to overcome gravity. Students observe fluid pooling in lower reservoirs and experience the physical work needed to perfuse the head.

Test B — Spaceflight Fluid Shift (Horizontal): Demonstrates the immediate cephalad fluid shift upon removal of gravity. Students measure the volume increase in the head chamber and correlate this with baroreceptor-mediated fluid excretion and the "puffy face" appearance observed in astronauts.

Test C — Return to Earth (Orthostatic Intolerance): Simulates post-flight orthostatic intolerance by removing approximately 15% of the fluid volume (representing space-induced blood volume loss) and returning the board to vertical orientation. Students observe how reduced fluid volume fails to adequately perfuse the head chamber, physically illustrating why astronauts experience dizziness and syncope upon landing.

Educational Objectives and Outcomes

This project achieves multiple educational objectives aligned with Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and STEM learning goals:

  1. Anatomical Understanding: Students construct a working model of the circulatory system, reinforcing knowledge of cardiac anatomy, vascular networks, and organ systems
  2. Physiological Comprehension: The model demonstrates homeostasis, blood pressure regulation, baroreceptor function, and cardiovascular adaptation to environmental change
  3. Physics Integration: Students apply principles of fluid dynamics, pressure gradients, and gravitational effects on fluid distribution
  4. Space Biology Awareness: The project introduces students to spaceflight physiology and NASA's ongoing research into astronaut health
  5. Scientific Inquiry: Students develop hypotheses, collect measurements, and draw evidence-based conclusions about cardiovascular function in altered gravitational environments
  6. Engineering Skills: Construction of the hydraulic system requires problem-solving, iterative design, and troubleshooting
